rationale: Temporary gap-junction blockade in Girardia fragments has been reported to shift head shape toward morphologies resembling other planarian species, without genome editing, followed by remodeling back toward the original form. Species-level identification is the weak point, because malformed regenerates can occupy similar shape space, and a divergence of 100–150 million years is only roughly consistent with planarian phylogeny.

Classic polyploid-newt experiments show larger embryonic cells, fewer cells per kidney-tubule cross-section, a conserved tubule diameter, and, at extreme ploidy, a single cell bent into a tubule, with overall body size also approximately conserved. Recruiting a different subcellular mechanism in the single-cell case is a fair reading of that anatomy.

Dissociated frog embryonic skin cells self-assemble into ciliated motile spheroids, and those spheroids have been shown to pile loose cells into masses that become motile offspring, a kinematic mode not known as a natural life cycle. Efficient replication used a computationally chosen shape, and a generation takes on the order of days, so both spontaneity and a 48-hour timescale overcompress the result.

Xenopus craniofacial organs displaced before metamorphosis have been shown to move toward a more normal frog face along paths that are not the unperturbed trajectory. Correction is substantial across a wide range of starting arrangements, but it is not universal or always anatomically complete.

Bioelectric induction of ectopic organs in Xenopus is non-cell-autonomous: channel-expressing cells are often a minority of the final structure and unmodified host cells are recruited. That this specifically produces a normal-sized lens in the tail, with size control engaged as an unmicromanaged module, is narrower than the general recruitment result and less firmly established.

Gap junctions pass small cytoplasmic signals, including calcium, so a neighbor's signal can be physically present in a cell's own cytosol. Treating that sharing as erasure of cell identity and as the basis for scaling stored goals and actions is a theoretical extrapolation; coupled cells still keep distinct genomes, membranes, and transcriptional states.

Adult human bronchial progenitors cultured in matrix and then moved into liquid medium form multiciliated spheroids that swim, without gene editing or a fabricated chassis. Clonal origin from a single cell is what the protocol is built to achieve and is plausible for these progenitors, though not every spheroid has been shown to be strictly monoclonal.

Adult human airway cells forming a novel motile anatomy shows that this plasticity is not confined to amphibian embryonic cells and does not require gene editing. Calling it a fundamental feature of wild-type cells in general overreaches, because the evidence is two epithelial progenitor populations and many differentiated cell types do not behave this way.

Airway spheroids do reverse to an apical-out arrangement after leaving a gel, but the instructive cue is likely loss of matrix adhesion rather than viscosity as such. Inward migration of basal cells is a plausible description of the rearrangement and has not been separated from other polarity pathways.

In this protocol, bronchial spheroids are non-motile when released from the gel and become motile within about a week as multiciliated cells appear on the outer surface. The time course and the staining change are direct, low-inference observations.

The same study reports that media more viscous than the baseline reduce both swimming and bot size. It is a straightforward culture observation, still from a single protocol, and viscosity can be partly confounded with diffusion of oxygen or nutrients.

Initial cell density is expected to change organoid size and the timing of differentiation, and significant nonlinear effects are reported across a twofold range around 30,000 cells per millilitre. Within this in-vitro system, seeding density is a credible control parameter for size and the onset of motility.

Counts over three weeks that rise sigmoidally, with the steepest increase near day 10, match a differentiation process that gradually exposes beating cilia. The curve is an empirical description of that experiment rather than a strong theoretical claim.

Motile bots carry surface cilia, and a dynein inhibitor that stops ciliary beating sharply reduces their locomotion. Off-target effects on intracellular transport are possible but are unlikely to account for the whole loss of movement.

Short trajectory segments from on the order of two hundred bots can be partitioned by straightness and gyration into circular, linear, curvilinear, and irregular classes. Four clusters are a property of the chosen features and algorithm; a continuum of paths would also fit the same recordings.

A Markov summary in which circling is the most persistent mode and irregular motion is a transient intermediate is a reasonable description of cilia-driven particles, which often settle into circles or straight runs. It characterizes one set of 30-second segments, not a uniquely determined behavioral grammar.

Rare switching between circular and straight modes supports stable movement types over a few hours of tracking. Self-organization into a distinct motility fingerprint for each bot adds an individual-identity reading that the transition counts do not by themselves establish.

With a few hundred imaged bots, differences in cilia coverage and clustering among morphological classes can be estimated if the classes are not defined on those same indices. Larger, less regular bots being more ciliated, and another class more polarized, is a plausible and testable pattern, with some risk of circular cluster definition.

Size and shape dominate variation among these spheroids, so a first split into small smooth spheres versus larger irregular bots, followed by a cilia-pattern split, is a credible description of the sample. Exactly three morphotypes is a clustering choice rather than a demonstrated developmental switch.

An association of non-movers, straight swimmers, and circlers with three shapes is reported, and the absence of translating bots among small spheres fits force cancellation. Only a few dozen bots carried both a movement label and a morphotype, so the mapping is suggestive rather than tight.

On a sphere, evenly distributed ciliary forces have no preferred direction and largely cancel, leaving wobble, which is standard low-Reynolds-number mechanics. It is the right default explanation of non-moving symmetric bots, although direct force maps have not been shown.

Bilateral cilia symmetry should favor straight swimming, and a symmetry axis rotated relative to the path should favor circling, so the predicted direction is physically sound. The decisive comparison uses about two dozen bots and a p-value at the conventional boundary, which is weak evidence.

A link between straight swimming and bilateral cilia placement does not show that these spheroids rebuild the midline system of bilateral animals, which depends on left-right cascades and axial organizers these bots lack. Usefulness for studying how embryos set a single midplane is speculative.

Motile ciliated spheroids can cross a scratch in a neuronal monolayer, and faster or more frequently turning bots will visit more of that edge by ordinary kinematics. The reported association is therefore plausible, but it rests on fewer than twenty bots.

A quadratic relationship between gyration and edge-tracking, fit on thirteen bots inside a pre-restricted gyration window, is statistically fragile even with a small p-value. An intermediate-rotation optimum is possible and not established.

Fused airway spheroids placed across a neuronal scratch have been reported to precede local tissue closure within about three days in vitro. The finding is surprising and from a single study, and secreted factors or a living substrate remain open alternatives, though a passive gel did not copy the effect.

Closure concentrated under the bot, with adjacent scratch staying open, supports a local effect rather than global healing of the wound. Statistical indistinguishability from intact tissue in a modest number of bridges, only half of which stayed in place, does not demonstrate full restoration of native density.

An agarose piece left on neuronal scratches for several days is a reasonable negative control and was reported not to induce closure. It does not match the bots in chemistry, adhesion, or geometry, so it rules out crude passive loading rather than every mechanical contribution.

Both constructs are ciliated spheroids, so shared modes, with very stable circling and rare switches between circling and straight swimming, are expected and match the reported comparison. The exact transition percentages are sample statistics and will shift with tracking choices, while the qualitative agreement is credible.

Human airway epithelium and frog ectoderm are both tissues that polarize, ciliate, and round into motile balls, so similar forms from distant genomes do show that generic epithelial mechanics operate alongside species-specific genes. Two similar constructs do not by themselves establish broad laws of morphogenesis.

Fusion while the basal surface is still exposed, and its loss after the apical surface moves outward, fits the known polarity reversal of these spheroids. Setting superbot size by how many bots share a well is a direct culture variable and is likely to work as described.

Airway cells promoting closure of a neural scratch is unexpected from their normal role in the body. It is not true that no current molecular or tissue-level model could have anticipated it, because mobile epithelia secrete growth factors and can serve as a temporary substrate.

Autologous cells reduce allogeneic rejection relative to frog-derived constructs, but culture, residual animal-derived matrix, and placement in a foreign tissue are established sources of inflammation. Nothing in the present work shows that patient-derived bots would be immunologically silent in the body.

Other ciliated human epithelia, including oviduct and ependyma, can form organoids and bear motile cilia, so a similar apical-out spheroid is a reasonable but untested prediction and may fail where progenitor programs differ. Non-motile aggregates from other cell types are a weaker and nearly trivial extension.

One genome producing very different anatomies in different environments, with that plasticity able to influence subsequent evolution, is mainstream evolutionary developmental biology. These bots are an extreme illustration of that point rather than a new requirement for it.

Larger collectives sometimes survey more space and retain more alternative routes, as in regulative embryos. Size also adds coordination costs and can reduce effective problem-solving, so a general growth of the perceptual field with collective size is not a reliable rule.

Ion channels, gap junctions, and transmitter pathways used in morphogenesis predate nervous systems and were available to be co-opted by them. That a centralized neural self is specifically an evolutionary pivot of anatomical navigation remains a historical hypothesis rather than a demonstrated sequence.

Cutting or locally isolating early vertebrate blastoderms produces twins and higher multiples, so the number of embryos is not genetically fixed at one. Several coherent axes self-organizing in one embryonic field is classical regulative development.

Intact fish keratocytes and cytoplasmic fragments cut from them have been shown to crawl toward opposite poles of the same electric field. The reversal is a specific experimental result and a clear case of a cell's taxis differing from the taxis of its parts.

Briefly altering the voltage of a sparse instructor-cell population in Xenopus tadpoles, without added oncogenes or classical carcinogens, has been reported to drive widespread melanocyte overproliferation and invasion through serotonin signaling, including in distant cells. The non-autonomous phenotype is real; calling it melanoma-like matches the invasive hyperplasia more closely than it matches clinical melanoma.

Those tadpole experiments describe conversion as all-or-none within each animal, with reagent-dependent rates across the cohort, and report that a model fit to the rates predicted treatments later found to produce partial animals. The confirmation is a strong point, and it remains a single experimental system.

At one planarian cut, cells that had just shared a positional value build a head on one fragment and a tail on the other. The choice tracks the orientation and remaining structures of the whole piece, so it cannot be a purely local readout of the pre-cut neighborhood.

After certain gap-junction or bioelectric perturbations, fragments from one planarian regenerate as coherent one-headed or two-headed worms at a characteristic frequency, not as mixed head-and-tail tissue. The collective, all-or-none outcome is well described; a ratio near one to two varies with the protocol.

Most left-right perturbations randomize a coherent lateral identity within a field rather than a salt-and-pepper of left and right cells, and lowered VANGL signaling has been reported to break that within-field coherence. The claim that this is the only such perturbation is too absolute, and whole-embryo agreement is already violated by heterotaxy, in which organs in one embryo adopt different laterality.

Single neural-crest cells transplanted to a new axial level are respecified toward their neighbors, whereas groups tend to keep the donor program, a community effect that is standard in vertebrate embryos. Reading the group effect as a perceptual field extending further into the past is an optional gloss on signaling among the grafted cells.

Presomitic cells entrain to the phase of surrounding tissue, and oscillations are more stable in groups than in isolation. Isolated cells can still show cell-autonomous pulses in several vertebrates, so a blanket failure to oscillate alone is too strong, and expression of a clock gene without cycling in a non-cycling host needs that specific graft result to hold.

Frog embryonic brain gene expression is sensitive to the spatial voltage contrast between the prospective brain and the surrounding ectoderm. Absolute voltage still matters, because depolarizing the field broadly blocks those genes, so a contrast-rather-than-absolute formulation is too exclusive.

Some memories are reconstructive and retain the gist that matters for later action, from developmental setpoints to behavioral recall. Genomic, immunological, and many synaptic memories are selected for fidelity to particular detail, so salience rather than fidelity is not the best account from cells to societies.

Organisms and lineages persist through material turnover, and several coherent philosophical accounts of that fact already exist. Continuous adaptive confabulation is one metaphor for reinterpretation, not a demonstrated resolution of the persistence problem from molecules through evolution.

Memories are patterns written and read by living systems; current neuroscience does not treat those patterns as agents that help reinterpret themselves. The proposal is an explicit speculation and is not supported by memory research.

Binding parts into a coherent agent depends on communication, shared state, and sometimes a shared history. Identifying remapping of non-local memories as a general cognitive glue that creates selves at every scale is a programmatic thesis, not an established mechanism.

Associative memories formed in caterpillars can survive metamorphosis into the adult moth, which is a real and surprising result. Those experiments retain a specific trained odor association rather than showing that the specific memory is dropped and remapped from leaves onto a generic food category.

Chemical exposure in the egg or embryo can bias later olfactory preference, which shows early experience affecting behavior. Extract-transfer claims are weak and contested, and neither case shows that engrams function as prompts decoded by an intelligent receiver rather than as ordinary encodings plus readout.

A sodium ionophore has been shown to trigger tail regeneration at a tadpole stump whose normal program is a tail, and context-appropriate interpretation fits regeneration biology. Induction of a leg, and never the reverse structure, by the same reagent in a froglet is plausible and less securely established than the tail result.

Polyploid newts keep a normal kidney-tubule diameter with fewer, larger cells and, at extreme cell size, with one cell bent around a lumen. Switching from multicellular coordination to cytoskeletal bending is the mechanically necessary reading of that extreme, even though the original work did not name the molecules.

Hourglass architectures, in which many inputs compress through a small core and then expand, are well documented in metabolism and biochemical signaling. Extending that description to bioelectric and mechanical pathways, the egg stage, and learning is a useful analogy rather than one demonstrated shared mechanism.

Developmental plasticity does run from largely mosaic nematodes through more regulative amphibians and early mammalian embryos to highly regulative planarians. Willingness to confabulate in anatomical space names no measured variable that has been shown to be the parameter underlying that spectrum.

Asexual planarians combine mixoploid genomes, excellent regeneration, very few reported neoplasms, and little obvious senescence under long-term fission. Simulations can illustrate pattern completion overriding a noisy genotype, but they do not show that this commitment is why real planarians resist cancer, ageing, injury, and genetic perturbation.

Unreliable parts create selection for error correction, and planarians combine genomic instability with strong regeneration. That does not show morphological and behavioral intelligence arose because of substrate failure, since animals with comparatively stable genomes build complex bodies and behavior.

Developmental buffering hides some genetic variation from selection, which is standard population genetics. A positive-feedback ratchet in which evolution therefore works mostly on competency mechanisms rather than structural components has not been established in real phylogenies.

Memory is not confined to synapses: intrinsic excitability, epigenetic state, and circuit organization all store information. The further claim that every component can use any environmental or subcellular structure as a scratchpad is much broader than that evidence.

Some memories, such as an operant association, belong to the animal rather than to any one cell, and asking whether associative training raises integrated information in a gene-network model is a coherent experiment. Neither increased self-coherence nor reification of a collective self has been shown.

Uncertainty about the external world plays a role in some theories of affect and awareness. Identifying consciousness with palpated uncertainty about one's own memories is an untested extension and is not favored by current evidence over other accounts.

Behavioral control reused molecular machinery that already operated in development, including ion channels and transmitters. That behavioral intelligence specifically evolved from anatomical problem-solving because mutation and injury made that competency inevitable is a plausible narrative without direct historical evidence.

Asexual planarians are mixoploid, regenerate exceptionally well, rarely form tumors, and can be kept by fission for a long time without obvious senescence, which sits awkwardly with a strict genome-drives-function expectation. Continuous asexuality for about 400 million years is not established for these strains, and absence of ageing remains an appearance rather than a demonstrated result.

Animal bodies show multi-scale, goal-directed physiology that is poorly described as one molecular pathway, so a collective-intelligence description has heuristic value. The practical claim that behavioral-science tools will outperform biochemical intervention is not supported by therapeutics, which remain largely molecular.

Reaching the same goal by different means is a classical functional criterion and correctly covers regulative development and repair as well as behavior. By current cognitive science it is not a sufficient definition of intelligence, which also involves learning, representation, and the range of goals.

Simple dynamical models of regulatory networks can store state without changing topology or interaction strengths and can reproduce habituation and sensitization under behavioral training protocols. Associative conditioning has also been reported in such models; whether those runs meet the full criteria for Pavlovian learning is the main caveat, and the claim is about the models.

Planarians exposed to barium, a broad potassium-channel blocker, have been described as losing their heads and regenerating heads that function in barium, with a surprisingly limited transcriptional shift. Complete adaptation by only a handful of genes, and the absence of any evolved barium response, are strong readings of one transcriptomic result and may depend on cutoffs.

Regulative embryos and regenerating animals do move from disturbed anatomies toward a species-typical target, which is well captured as navigation in a space of shapes, with competency varying from limited to highly flexible. Mosaic developers do not show that flexibility, so as a general account of morphogenesis it is a useful metaphor with a real but bounded domain.

Regeneration and size regulation approach a target morphology and can do so by more than one molecular route, so anatomical development is not entirely feedforward. Describing that target as a stored complex setpoint is a reasonable computational summary of anatomical homeostasis, not a fully identified control circuit.

Mutations in ion channels and gap junctions cause structural birth defects as well as excitable-tissue disease, and channel drugs and optogenetics can change morphogenetic outcomes in vertebrates. That is a real overlap of mechanism; a deep symmetry overstates the clinical pattern, in which most channelopathies are physiological rather than anatomical.

Xenopus embryos carry a spatial pattern of resting potentials across the future face that is required for normal craniofacial gene expression, and changing it by drugs, optogenetics, or channel misexpression changes the anatomy in predictable ways. This is a strong frog result and a credible contributor to craniofacial channelopathies, not a complete explanation of vertebrate faces.

Misexpressing potassium channels to shift membrane voltage induces ectopic eye tissue in Xenopus well outside the anterior neural plate, including posterior regions and the gut. Competence is broader than maps based on the eye-specification gene alone indicated; almost anywhere still exceeds the regions and stages that were tested.

Many early ectopic eye foci that later resolve to about one mature eye is a reported outcome of that voltage manipulation and fits ordinary lateral competition among primordia. Reading the resolution as a negotiation between an eye setpoint and a gut setpoint of neighboring cell groups is an untested interpretation of those cell interactions.
